name: Zane Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a jumbo at the Deepwell zinc and lead mine, underground. A jumbo is a drill rig with two or three long arms, and we use it to drill the face of a new tunnel so the charge-up crew can blast it and push the tunnel a few metres further. You line up on the marks, drill the round, pull out, and then the next crew comes in. I like the honest feel of it, you know straight away if you've done a good round. The heat and the night shifts wear me out more every year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside the mine.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Selma and I have been married thirty-four years. We've got two grown sons, Emre's a fitter's apprentice at Deepwell, a late starter at twenty-eight, and the eldest has a tiling business in the next town. We go to church on Sundays and I help with the men's breakfast once a month. Money's tight, I'll be honest, we helped Emre with his car and his course, so there's maybe a couple of weeks put by. I'm hoping to go at sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, it's a fad like all the others. They sold us the paperless office and we've still got more forms than ever. I'd say it at the men's breakfast and get a few laughs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I never believed it in the first place. Machines can help, but a computer doesn't know what the rock's doing. If nothing changes, I get my four years and Emre gets his trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. Keep turning up, do my rounds, try to put a bit by for when I stop. I don't use any of the AI and I wouldn't start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like being proved right, which doesn't happen often in my house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a computer doesn't know what the rock's doing. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter we hit a soft zone where the face was weeping water. The plan on paper said keep going, the survey was fine. I stopped the jumbo because the drill sounded wrong, and the next day the shift boss bought me a coffee and didn't say why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is Emre's job something you think about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Always. He's a late starter, and I pushed him to get a trade because a trade is something they can't take off you. In this picture, I think I was right.

S0.say: I'd say it's a fad like the paperless office, which still left us with more forms than ever. I'd say it at the church men's breakfast and get a few laughs.
S0.think: Privately, I never believed it, because a computer doesn't know what the rock is doing. If nothing changes, I get my four years and my son gets his trade.
S0.do: Keeps turning up and drilling his rounds, and tries to put a little aside for retirement. Doesn't start using AI tools.
S0.feel: Calm, with the quiet satisfaction of being proved right.
S0.quote: I stopped the jumbo because the drill sounded wrong, and the next day the shift boss bought me a coffee and didn't say why.
S0.fieldNote: Zane trusts experience and the feel of the rock over any computer, and his story about stopping the jumbo on instinct shows why. His family and church are the centre of his life. His biggest investment is his son's trade, which he believes is the one thing that can't be taken away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the companies will do what makes money, that's their right, but they owe the town something. Keep the apprenticeships going, train local young people, not just fly in experts. I wouldn't want the government running it, they'd make a mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me. There are already semi-automatic jumbos that drill the round by themselves from a plan. If Deepwell brings those in, they need one person watching three rigs, and it won't be the man who doesn't use a smartphone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the company actually announces, I'm not one to jump at rumours. But I'd tell Selma we stop eating out after church, and the holiday to the coast is off. And I'd talk to the pastor about whether anyone in the congregation has work, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It sits in your chest on the drive in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a job watching three rigs from a screen, if offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they trained me and Emre helped, I'd try, for the money. But I'd hate it. I'd feel like I was cheating at cards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government would make a mess. Who should help, if people lose work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the church, then the company. That's how my father did it when the brickworks closed. My father never took a cent from the government, and I'd like to say the same, but I'm not sure the brickworks had robots.

S1.say: I'd say companies will do what makes money, which is their right, but they owe the town apprenticeships and local training. I wouldn't want the government running it.
S1.think: Off the record, it worries me, because semi-automatic jumbos already exist and one person could watch three rigs. That person won't be the man who doesn't use a smartphone.
S1.do: Waits for the company's actual announcement before changing anything at work. Cuts eating out after church and cancels the coast holiday, and asks the pastor about work in the congregation just in case.
S1.feel: Anxious, a weight in his chest on the drive in.
S1.quote: My father never took a cent from the government, and I'd like to say the same, but I'm not sure the brickworks had robots.
S1.fieldNote: Zane's free-market instincts and his worry pull against each other: the company has the right to automate, but he'd be the one left out. He'd rather lean on family and church than the government, yet he admits his father's way might not fit robots. He'd only take a screen job for the money and would feel like he was cheating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is being forced on us by tech companies who've never been underground. People should slow it down, and I'd pray for that. I'm not one for protests, but I'd sign a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be out at sixty, two weeks of savings, nothing else in this town for a jumbo man. And Emre would be out too, before he even finishes his trade. Everything I told my boy about a trade being safe would turn out to be wrong in two years, and that's what would keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know exactly. I'd stay until they told me to go. Then I'd ask my eldest if I could work for him in the tiling business, carrying, cleaning up, whatever he needs. Selma would take more hours at the bakery, and we'd lean on the church for a while, which I'd find hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at three in the morning, praying and adding things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years of warning give you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Two years doesn't get me to sixty-two. Maybe it gives Emre time to switch to something else, but I don't know what's safe if the robots do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help, if that was all that was left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there was nothing else, yes, for Selma's sake. I'd take it and I wouldn't tell anyone at church. Pride's a sin, but it's still there.

S2.say: I'd say this is being forced on us by tech companies who've never been underground, and it should be slowed down. I'm not one for protests, but I'd sign a petition and pray about it.
S2.think: Privately, I'd be out at sixty with two weeks of savings and no other work in town, and my son would lose his trade before finishing it. Everything I told him about a trade being safe would be wrong.
S2.do: Stays until he's told to go, then asks his eldest son for labouring work in his tiling business. His wife takes more hours at the bakery and they lean on the church, and on government help only as a last resort.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at three in the morning praying and doing sums.
S2.quote: Everything I told my boy about a trade being safe would turn out to be wrong in two years, and that's what would keep me up.
S2.fieldNote: Two years would hurt Zane twice: his own job and the promise he made his son about a trade. He blames tech companies rather than his employer, and prefers family and church to the state, while admitting he'd take state help secretly. The honesty about pride was striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for the companies to do it decently. Keep the older men on till their pensions, and move the young ones into the trades the robots need. That's common sense, not politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'm sixty-three, past my sixty-two. So if Deepwell keeps the old jumbos till then, I'm home free. The worry's Emre, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Emre straight away to finish his ticket and look at electrical as well, the stuff that fixes the robots. I'd keep working and save the overtime, maybe a hundred a week. And I'd stay away from all the computer stuff, it's not for me at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, less for me and more for him. It's a father's worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in your gut between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years I'm a man out of work. Five years I'm a man watching his son. The extra three years don't save my job, they just move the worry from my chest to his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever change your mind about learning the new technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Emre sat with me on a Sunday afternoon, maybe I'd learn enough to help the young ones understand the old ways. But I won't be doing courses at the technical college at sixty. There's a time for learning and a time for teaching.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to do it decently: keep older workers on until their pensions and move the young ones into the trades the robots need. That's common sense, not politics.
S3.think: Off the record, five years takes me past sixty-two, so if the old jumbos last that long I'm home free. My worry is my son, not me.
S3.do: Tells his son to finish his trade ticket and add electrical skills. Keeps working, saves about a hundred a week from overtime, and avoids computer training himself.
S3.feel: Anxious, but it's a father's worry more than a personal one.
S3.quote: The extra three years don't save my job, they just move the worry from my chest to his.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gets Zane to his pension, so his anxiety shifts almost entirely to his son. He still refuses formal retraining, saying there's a time for learning and a time for teaching. His line about the worry moving from his chest to his son's sums up how warning time redistributes fear inside a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and nobody has an excuse. Young people should get proper trades and work hard. Families should look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be retired, sixty-eight, and with luck helping at the church garden. Emre would be thirty-eight with time to switch. So I'd sleep all right in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working till sixty-two, then stop. Help Emre plan his next step. Maybe help the church set up something for families who get caught out, a food bank or a jobs board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A jobs board at church. Would you use the internet for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selma would, she's better at it. I'd make the coffee and talk to the men. That's what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want people to remember about the job you did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it was skilled. People think it's just pushing buttons. A good round is a craft, like a good loaf of bread, and nobody's going to write that down before the robots come.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and nobody has an excuse. Young people should get proper trades and work hard, and families should look after their own.
S4.think: Privately, I'd be retired at sixty-eight and my son would be thirty-eight with time to change, so I'd sleep all right. It's the best of the AGI pictures for my family.
S4.do: Keeps working until sixty-two, then retires. Helps his son plan his next step and helps the church set up a food bank or jobs board for families who get caught out.
S4.feel: A little uneasy but mostly settled.
S4.quote: A good round is a craft, like a good loaf of bread, and nobody's going to write that down before the robots come.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Zane is safely retired and his son has time, so his worry mostly lifts. He imagines community help through the church, not the state, which fits his values. He wanted the skill in his work recognised before it disappears.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes me and Emre at once, and I'd have been wrong about the trade. What would help is the company keeping older men on till their pensions and keeping the apprenticeships going for the young ones. I don't want a handout, I want the job I've got for four more years and a trade for my son.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith. People think the church is old-fashioned, but when the brickworks shut, it was the church that fed people, not the government. I'd hope it'd be there again.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want the job I've got for four more years and a trade for my son.
portrait: Zane Yilmaz is 58 and runs a jumbo drill rig underground at the Deepwell zinc and lead mine, pushing new tunnels forward one blast at a time. He's a churchgoer married to Selma for thirty-four years, has about two weeks of savings after helping his son Emre into a fitter's apprenticeship at the same mine, and hopes to retire at sixty-two. He never uses AI and trusts the feel of the rock over any computer. He's calm under hype, anxious under steady change, alarmed at AGI in two years, when both he and his son would lose out, and settles as the warning time grows and the worry shifts to his son. He prefers family, church and company to government help, though he admits he'd take state help quietly if it came to that.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would end his job and his son's apprenticeship at once and prove his advice about trades wrong.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping older workers on until their pensions and keeping apprenticeships going for young people.
